lesson.title: Can They Interbreed? The Biological Species Concept
lesson.summary: The biological species concept defines a species as a group of populations whose members can actually or potentially interbreed and produce fertile offspring in nature, a definition that works well for many sexually reproducing organisms but breaks down for asexual organisms, fossils, and a few unusual real world cases.
lesson.body:
Given everything covered so far in this unit, drift, founder effects, bottlenecks, gene flow, mutation, and the several modes of natural selection, a natural question arises: at what point do two populations that have been changing independently actually become two different species? The most widely taught answer is the biological species concept, formalized by evolutionary biologist Ernst Mayr, which defines a species as a group of actually or potentially interbreeding natural populations that are reproductively isolated from other such groups. The key phrase is reproductive isolation. Members of the same species can interbreed with each other and produce offspring that are themselves fertile, while members of different species either cannot interbreed at all, or if they do produce hybrid offspring, those hybrids are typically sterile, weak, or otherwise unable to pass genes back into either parent population. Horses and donkeys illustrate the point cleanly. The two can mate and produce mules, but mules are almost always sterile, because horses and donkeys carry different numbers of chromosomes that cannot pair up properly during the formation of the mule's own gametes. That sterility is what keeps horse genes and donkey genes from actually mixing into a shared gene pool, which is precisely why horses and donkeys count as separate species under this definition despite being able to produce offspring together.

This definition ties directly back to gene flow. Under the biological species concept, a species is, in effect, defined by the boundary of its gene pool: individuals within the species are connected by actual or potential interbreeding, meaning alleles can flow freely among them, while individuals in a different species are cut off from that gene flow by some barrier to successful reproduction. That barrier is what allows the variation within each species, the product of mutation, selection, and drift acting inside each one separately, to accumulate as differences between species rather than being blended back together the way ongoing gene flow would blend it within a single species.

Useful as it is, the biological species concept has real, well recognized limitations. It simply does not apply to organisms that reproduce asexually, such as most bacteria and some plants, since the entire definition is built around interbreeding, and an organism that does not breed sexually at all has no interbreeding to test. It also cannot be applied to fossils, since there is no way to test whether two long dead organisms could have interbred, so paleontologists must fall back on physical similarity instead, a different and less precise standard. A further complication comes from ring species: a chain of neighboring populations, distributed for example around a mountain range or a valley, in which each population along the chain can interbreed with its immediate neighbors, but the two populations at the ends of the chain, where it finally comes back around on itself, cannot interbreed with each other even though they are connected the whole way around by a continuous sequence of interbreeding neighbors. Ring species make clear that reproductive isolation is not always a clean yes or no boundary between two groups. It can be a matter of degree that changes gradually across geography, which is exactly why biologists keep more than one species concept in their toolkit rather than relying on just this one.
